updates.explanation: The source lists delayed portal venous filling and narrowed SMA/intramural branches as non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia clues. Watershed areas are favoured, although small bowel may also be involved. Involved segments are often thickened rather than always thin. Pampiniform plexus dilation describes varicocele.

updates.question_text: Regarding nutcracker syndrome consequences and diagnosis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Left gonadal venous drainage explains associated left testicular pain in men and left lower quadrant pain in women
It always requires immediate open aortic repair
It presents as a high-flow pulmonary AVM syndrome
Retrograde venography with renal-caval pressure measurements is described as the diagnostic gold standard
It characteristically causes bilateral arm swelling from SVC obstruction
options_after: Left gonadal venous drainage explains associated left testicular pain in men and left lower quadrant pain in women
It characteristically requires immediate open aortic repair
It presents as a high-flow pulmonary AVM syndrome
Retrograde venography with renal-caval pressure measurements is described as the diagnostic gold standard
It characteristically causes bilateral arm swelling from SVC obstruction
updates.explanation: Because the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, nutcracker compression can produce left-sided gonadal venous symptoms. The source gives retrograde venography with renal-caval pressure measurements as the diagnostic gold standard. It is not an indication for open aortic repair, pulmonary AVM workup or SVC syndrome evaluation.

updates.question_text: Regarding testicular varicocele, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is abnormal dilatation of veins in the pampiniform plexus
Left-sided predominance relates to the left testicular vein draining into the left renal vein at a right angle
Most idiopathic varicoceles are left-sided in the source
All left-sided varicoceles in adults require abdominal CT for malignancy search
Right-sided varicocele in an adult is always physiologic and needs no attention
options_after: It is abnormal dilatation of veins in the pampiniform plexus
Left-sided predominance relates to the left testicular vein draining into the left renal vein at a right angle
Most idiopathic varicoceles are left-sided in the source
Most left-sided varicoceles in adults require abdominal CT for malignancy search
Right-sided varicocele in an adult is characteristically physiologic and does not need attention
updates.explanation: Varicocele is dilatation of the pampiniform venous plexus and is usually left-sided, related to left gonadal venous anatomy and left renal vein drainage. Isolated left varicocele is commonly benign and does not automatically require cancer-hunting imaging. New isolated right-sided or non-decompressible varicocele in an adult should prompt concern for abdominal or pelvic pathology.

updates.question_text: Regarding concerning varicocele patterns and next imaging, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Bilateral decompressive varicoceles always require urgent abdominal CT for cancer search
Non-decompressible varicocele is a concerning pattern in the source
New isolated right-sided varicocele in an adult should raise concern for abdominal or pelvic malignancy
Abdominal CT, MRI or ultrasound is appropriate when malignancy search is needed
Left renal malignancy invading the renal vein can cause a concerning varicocele pattern
options_after: Bilateral decompressive varicoceles characteristically require urgent abdominal CT for cancer search
Non-decompressible varicocele is a concerning pattern in the source
New isolated right-sided varicocele in an adult should raise concern for abdominal or pelvic malignancy
Abdominal CT, MRI or ultrasound is appropriate when malignancy search is needed
Left renal malignancy invading the renal vein can cause a concerning varicocele pattern
updates.explanation: The source highlights non-decompressible varicocele and new isolated right-sided varicocele in adults as concerning patterns that should trigger abdominal or pelvic imaging. Left renal malignancy invading the renal vein is one possible mechanism. Bilateral decompressive varicoceles may require treatment in infertility but are not the classic cancer-search scenario.

updates.question_text: Regarding radiology-facing vasculitis pattern recognition, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Wall thickening, occlusion, dilatation and aneurysm formation can overlap across vasculitides
All vasculitides are distinguished primarily by the number of pulmonary nodules
Age, sex and vessel distribution help separate otherwise similar imaging patterns
Large-vessel vasculitis includes Takayasu arteritis and giant cell arteritis in the source summary
ANCA status is irrelevant to small-vessel vasculitis classification in the source
options_after: Wall thickening, occlusion, dilatation and aneurysm formation can overlap across vasculitides
Most vasculitides are distinguished primarily by the number of pulmonary nodules
Age, sex and vessel distribution help separate otherwise similar imaging patterns
Large-vessel vasculitis includes Takayasu arteritis and giant cell arteritis in the source summary
ANCA status is irrelevant to small-vessel vasculitis classification in the source
updates.explanation: The source states that many vasculitides can look similar on imaging, with wall thickening, occlusions, dilatations and aneurysms. The practical discriminators are patient demographics, involved vessels and clinical context. It groups Takayasu and giant cell arteritis as large-vessel vasculitides. ANCA status is part of the small-vessel classification rather than irrelevant.

updates.question_text: Regarding Takayasu arteritis, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is primarily a disease of isolated temporal artery wall thickening in older patients
It classically affects young Asian women in the source framing
The source states that pulmonary arteries are never involved
Its hallmark is a post-catheter pulmonary artery pseudoaneurysm
Aortic and major branch involvement should suggest the diagnosis
options_after: It is primarily a disease of isolated temporal artery wall thickening in older patients
It classically affects young Asian women in the source framing
The source states that pulmonary arteries are not involved
Its hallmark is a post-catheter pulmonary artery pseudoaneurysm
Aortic and major branch involvement should suggest the diagnosis
updates.explanation: Takayasu arteritis is framed as a large-vessel vasculitis in young Asian women, with aortic and major branch involvement. Acute disease can show wall thickening and enhancement, while later disease can show diffuse narrowing. Temporal artery disease in older patients suggests giant cell arteritis. Pulmonary artery involvement can occur, classically with peripheral pruning.

updates.question_text: Regarding carotid stenosis Doppler thresholds in the source, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Normal ICA peak systolic velocity is described as less than 125 cm/s
ICA/CCA ratio and end-diastolic velocity are not used for carotid stenosis grading in the source
A 50-69% stenosis is associated with ICA PSV in the 125-230 cm/s range
Greater than 70% stenosis is associated with ICA PSV above 230 cm/s
Less than 50% stenosis always produces a marked peak systolic velocity rise
options_after: Normal ICA peak systolic velocity is described as less than 125 cm/s
ICA/CCA ratio and end-diastolic velocity are not used for carotid stenosis grading in the source
A 50-69% stenosis is associated with ICA PSV in the 125-230 cm/s range
Greater than 70% stenosis is associated with ICA PSV above 230 cm/s
Less than 50% stenosis characteristically produces a marked peak systolic velocity rise
updates.explanation: The source gives the standard carotid Doppler pattern: normal ICA PSV below 125 cm/s, 50-69% stenosis around 125-230 cm/s, and greater than 70% stenosis above 230 cm/s. ICA/CCA ratio and ICA EDV are additional grading parameters rather than irrelevant. Less than 50% stenosis is stated not to alter the peak systolic velocity.

updates.question_text: Regarding proximal stenosis clues on carotid Doppler, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Unilateral tardus-parvus always proves internal carotid artery occlusion
Unilateral tardus-parvus waveform suggests innominate artery stenosis in the source
Bilateral tardus-parvus is the classic isolated external carotid artery waveform
Tardus-parvus is unrelated to upstream disease
Bilateral tardus-parvus waveform suggests aortic stenosis in the source
options_after: Unilateral tardus-parvus characteristically proves internal carotid artery occlusion
Unilateral tardus-parvus waveform suggests innominate artery stenosis in the source
Bilateral tardus-parvus is the classic isolated external carotid artery waveform
Tardus-parvus is unrelated to upstream disease
Bilateral tardus-parvus waveform suggests aortic stenosis in the source
updates.explanation: The source's proximal stenosis trick is that unilateral tardus-parvus suggests innominate stenosis, whereas bilateral tardus-parvus suggests aortic stenosis. Tardus-parvus reflects downstream effects of upstream stenosis. ICA occlusion and ECA waveform identification use different Doppler features.

updates.question_text: Regarding subclavian steal on ultrasound, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It involves proximal subclavian stenosis or occlusion
Early steal always means complete retrograde vertebral flow throughout the cardiac cycle
Retrograde flow in the ipsilateral vertebral artery is a key finding
A high-velocity subclavian stenosis may be demonstrated
It is defined by absent diastolic flow from brain death
options_after: It involves proximal subclavian stenosis or occlusion
Early steal characteristically means complete retrograde vertebral flow throughout the cardiac cycle
Retrograde flow in the ipsilateral vertebral artery is a key finding
A high-velocity subclavian stenosis may be demonstrated
It is defined by absent diastolic flow from brain death
updates.explanation: The source describes subclavian steal as proximal subclavian stenosis/occlusion with retrograde ipsilateral vertebral flow and a high-velocity subclavian stenosis. Early steal is a spectrum finding and may show mid-systolic deceleration while late systolic flow remains antegrade, so it is not necessarily complete retrograde flow throughout the cycle. Brain death Doppler physiology is a different topic.

updates.question_text: Regarding LVAD Doppler waveforms, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: LVAD waveform spikes are always larger than a normal ICA waveform
LVAD causes the vertebral artery to become permanently retrograde
LVAD waveform interpretation is based on temporal tap response
LVAD arterial waveforms become mostly flat with continuous systolic and diastolic flow
LVAD is diagnosed by renal microaneurysms
options_after: LVAD waveform spikes are characteristically larger than a normal ICA waveform
LVAD causes the vertebral artery to become permanently retrograde
LVAD waveform interpretation is based on temporal tap response
LVAD arterial waveforms become mostly flat with continuous systolic and diastolic flow
LVAD is diagnosed by renal microaneurysms
updates.explanation: The source describes LVAD waveforms as losing the normal high-resistance spiked appearance and becoming relatively flat with continuous flow through systole and diastole. Small residual systolic spikes may reflect residual ventricular function. Retrograde vertebral flow suggests subclavian steal, and renal microaneurysms suggest PAN.

updates.question_text: Regarding carotid Doppler interpretation strategy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Distribution matters: unilateral versus bilateral waveform abnormality changes the differential
ICA/ECA differentiation depends only on vessel size and never on waveform resistance
A distal intracranial aneurysm reliably produces a proximal carotid waveform abnormality
The direction of vertebral flow is critical when evaluating suspected subclavian steal
Aortic valve disease cannot affect carotid Doppler waveforms
options_after: Distribution matters: unilateral versus bilateral waveform abnormality changes the differential
ICA/ECA differentiation depends primarily on vessel size and not on waveform resistance
A distal intracranial aneurysm reliably produces a proximal carotid waveform abnormality
The direction of vertebral flow is critical when evaluating suspected subclavian steal
Aortic valve disease will not affect carotid Doppler waveforms
updates.explanation: The source repeatedly uses distribution and waveform direction as practical interpretation tools. Unilateral versus bilateral abnormality helps separate innominate or subclavian disease from aortic valve disease, and vertebral flow direction is central to subclavian steal. ICA/ECA differentiation relies heavily on resistance and diastolic flow, while distal aneurysm may not alter proximal carotid flow.

updates.question_text: Regarding needle, catheter and sheath sizing, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: For needles, a smaller gauge number means a larger needle
Guidewire diameter is expressed in centimetres
French size for catheters refers to the external diameter
Sheath size refers to the inner lumen capacity
A larger gauge number always means a larger puncture needle
options_after: For needles, a smaller gauge number means a larger needle
Guidewire diameter is expressed in centimetres
French size for catheters refers to the external diameter
Sheath size refers to the inner lumen capacity
A larger gauge number characteristically means a larger puncture needle
updates.explanation: The source emphasises the counterintuitive gauge system: lower gauge number means larger needle. Catheter French size refers to external diameter, while sheath size refers to the internal capacity it can accommodate. Wire diameters are expressed in inches, whereas wire lengths are usually expressed in centimetres.

updates.question_text: Regarding French size and catheter dimensions, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: A 6 French catheter has an external diameter of 6 mm
3 French is approximately 1 mm in external diameter
French size describes guidewire length
The internal lumen of a catheter always equals its French size
Diameter in millimetres can be estimated as French size divided by 3
options_after: A 6 French catheter has an external diameter of 6 mm
3 French is approximately 1 mm in external diameter
French size describes guidewire length
The internal lumen of a catheter characteristically equals its French size
Diameter in millimetres can be estimated as French size divided by 3
updates.explanation: The source gives the practical conversion that 3F equals about 1 mm, so catheter external diameter in millimetres is French size divided by 3. A 6F catheter is therefore about 2 mm externally, not 6 mm. Wire length is given in centimetres, and catheter internal lumen must be checked separately.

updates.question_text: Regarding the skin puncture created by a vascular sheath, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The skin hole is larger than the labelled sheath size because the sheath wall adds thickness
The puncture size is identical to guidewire diameter regardless of sheath size
A 6F sheath may create a skin hole closer to an 8F outer diameter
A coaxial sheath-within-sheath setup requires accounting for both inner capacity and outer wall thickness
Sheath labelling uses the same convention as needle gauge
options_after: The skin hole is larger than the labelled sheath size because the sheath wall adds thickness
The puncture size is closely comparable to guidewire diameter despite variation in sheath size
A 6F sheath may create a skin hole closer to an 8F outer diameter
A coaxial sheath-within-sheath setup requires accounting for both inner capacity and outer wall thickness
Sheath labelling uses the same convention as needle gauge
updates.explanation: Because sheaths are labelled by inner lumen, the outer wall increases the skin puncture size. The source uses the practical rule that a labelled 6F sheath may behave like about 8F externally. Coaxial systems require a second step of thinking because the outer size of one sheath must fit into the inner lumen of the next sheath.

updates.question_text: Regarding micropuncture access, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Initial puncture is performed with a smaller 21G needle in the source
A 21G needle accepts a 0.018 inch guidewire
Micropuncture always provides more support than a standard 0.035 wire system
Micropuncture can be useful in anatomically sensitive areas such as internal jugular or dialysis access
The system can be exchanged up to a standard 4F-5F setup
options_after: Initial puncture is performed with a smaller 21G needle in the source
A 21G needle accepts a 0.018 inch guidewire
Micropuncture characteristically provides more support than a standard 0.035 wire system
Micropuncture can be useful in anatomically sensitive areas such as internal jugular or dialysis access
The system can be exchanged up to a standard 4F-5F setup
updates.explanation: Micropuncture starts with a 21G needle and 0.018 inch wire, then can be exchanged through dilators to a standard 4F-5F system. The source highlights difficult access and sensitive anatomy as useful settings. The tradeoff is that the 0.018 wire may not provide enough support when upsizing or advancing dilators.

updates.question_text: Regarding non-steerable and steerable guidewires, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Non-steerable wires are mainly supportive rails for catheters
Non-steerable wires are preferred for crossing stenoses and selecting small branches
Hydrophilic coating makes a wire less useful in tortuous or stenotic vessels
Steerable wires have shaped tips that can help select branches or negotiate tight spaces
All guidewires are intended to be steered without a catheter
options_after: Non-steerable wires are mainly supportive rails for catheters
Non-steerable wires are preferred for crossing stenoses and selecting small branches
Hydrophilic coating makes a wire less useful in tortuous or stenotic vessels
Steerable wires have shaped tips that can help select branches or negotiate tight spaces
Most guidewires are intended to be steered without a catheter
updates.explanation: The source divides guidewires into non-steerable support rails and steerable wires with shaped tips. Hydrophilic steerable wires are particularly useful for small, stenotic or tortuous targets. Stiff or non-steerable wires should not be treated as branch-selection tools, and stiff wires should be introduced through catheters.

updates.question_text: Regarding hydrophilic guidewires, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: They are designed to be kept dry for maximal performance
They are slippery when wet and sticky when dry
They should be wiped with a wet sponge during use in the source's next-step framing
They are used only as non-steerable rails for aortic stent grafting
They are useful when trying to enter a tight stenosis, small vessel or abscess cavity
options_after: They are designed to be kept dry for maximal performance
They are slippery when wet and sticky when dry
They should be wiped with a wet sponge during use in the source's next-step framing
They are used primarily as non-steerable rails for aortic stent grafting
They are useful when trying to enter a tight stenosis, small vessel or abscess cavity
updates.explanation: Hydrophilic wires are sticky dry and slippery wet, so the source stresses keeping them wet during use. Their main practical value is entering tight spaces: stenoses, small/tortuous vessels or abscess cavities. Lunderquist-type stiff wires, not hydrophilic crossing wires, are the source's archetype for aortic stent-graft rail support.

updates.question_text: Regarding guidewire length, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Guidewire length is usually expressed in centimetres
Wire diameter is usually expressed in centimetres
A 180 cm wire is never used for standard work
A 260 cm wire is useful for catheter exchange when extra length is needed
Minimal wire length is unrelated to catheter length or intravascular wire length
options_after: Guidewire length is usually expressed in centimetres
Wire diameter is usually expressed in centimetres
A 180 cm wire is not used for standard work
A 260 cm wire is useful for catheter exchange when extra length is needed
Minimal wire length is unrelated to catheter length or intravascular wire length
updates.explanation: The source distinguishes wire diameter in inches from wire length in centimetres. Standard wires are often around 180 cm, while 260 cm wires help when exchanging catheters or working from long access routes. The minimum wire length must cover catheter length plus the wire length already inside the patient.

updates.question_text: Regarding floppy guidewire tips, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: A 1 cm floppy tip is safer than a 6 cm floppy tip for avoiding dissection
Floppy tip length has no relationship to vessel injury risk in the source
The source states that all wires have identical tip stiffness
A shorter floppy segment increases the chance of vessel dissection compared with a longer floppy segment
A long floppy tip should never be chosen in a vessel
options_after: A 1 cm floppy tip is safer than a 6 cm floppy tip for avoiding dissection
Floppy tip length lacks relationship to vessel injury risk in the source
The source states that most wires have closely comparable tip stiffness
A shorter floppy segment increases the chance of vessel dissection compared with a longer floppy segment
A long floppy tip should not be chosen in a vessel
updates.explanation: The source's practical rule is that shorter floppy tips carry higher dissection risk than longer floppy tips. A 1 cm floppy tip is therefore riskier than a 6 cm floppy tip. Longer floppy tips are generally preferred unless the operator needs to enter a particularly tight target.

updates.question_text: Regarding stiff guidewires, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: They should be introduced through a catheter that was placed over a conventional guidewire
They are the first choice for selecting small tortuous branch vessels
They have lower dissection risk than floppy wires
They should not be steered through even mild curves in the source
They are identical in use to hydrophilic crossing wires
options_after: They should be introduced through a catheter that was placed over a conventional guidewire
They are the first choice for selecting small tortuous branch vessels
They have lower dissection risk than floppy wires
They should not be steered through even mild curves in the source
They are closely comparable in use to hydrophilic crossing wires
updates.explanation: The source explicitly warns that stiff guidewires should not be steered through curves and should be introduced through a catheter already placed over a conventional wire. Their role is support, not delicate branch selection. Increased stiffness increases the risk of dissection.

updates.question_text: Regarding angiographic catheter package numbers, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: A catheter labelled with 0.035 inner diameter accepts a 0.038 wire
The outer diameter size is given in French
The largest number on the package is always the catheter French size
The catheter length is given in centimetres
The inner diameter is given in inches and determines compatible wire size
options_after: A catheter labelled with 0.035 inner diameter accepts a 0.038 wire
The outer diameter size is given in French
The largest number on the package is characteristically the catheter French size
The catheter length is given in centimetres
The inner diameter is given in inches and determines compatible wire size
updates.explanation: The source describes three catheter package numbers: outer diameter in French, length in centimetres, and inner diameter in inches. The internal diameter determines the largest guidewire that can pass. A 0.035 catheter accepts a 0.035 or smaller wire, not a 0.038 wire.

updates.question_text: Regarding non-selective catheters, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Their primary role is selecting tiny distal hepatic branches
They should be used for embolotherapy into tiny vessels
They are used to inject contrast into medium and large vessels
They are always end-hole only catheters
They are also called flush catheters
options_after: Their primary role is selecting tiny distal hepatic branches
They should be used for embolotherapy into tiny vessels
They are used to inject contrast into medium and large vessels
They are characteristically end-hole primarily catheters
They are also called flush catheters
updates.explanation: Non-selective catheters are flush catheters used for medium and large vessel injections. Tiny distal vessel selection and embolotherapy are roles for selective catheters or microcatheters, not non-selective flush catheters. Non-selective pigtail and straight catheters may have side and end holes.

updates.question_text: Regarding pigtail catheters, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: They are primarily designed for superselective embolisation of tiny branches
They should be used in very small low-flow vessels without test injection
The curled distal morphology helps keep the catheter out of small branch vessels
They have no side holes in the source
They are defined by a hydrophilic guidewire coating
options_after: They are primarily designed for superselective embolisation of tiny branches
They should be used in very small low-flow vessels without test injection
The curled distal morphology helps keep the catheter out of small branch vessels
They lack side holes in the source
They are defined by a hydrophilic guidewire coating
updates.explanation: The pigtail is a non-selective flush catheter for larger vessels. Its curled shape helps prevent branch-vessel entry, and the source recommends a test injection before full injection to ensure the catheter is not in or against a small branch. It is not a superselective embolisation catheter and is not defined by wire coating.

updates.question_text: Regarding selective catheter hole configuration, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: End-hole-only selective catheters are suitable for hand injection
End-hole-only catheters are preferred for high-flow pump injection in tiny branches
End-hole-only selective catheters are useful for diagnostic angiography and embolisation procedures
Side-plus-end-hole selective catheters can tolerate pump-injected runs better
Side-plus-end-hole selective catheters should not be used for embolotherapy because material can exit side holes or become trapped
options_after: End-hole-only selective catheters are suitable for hand injection
End-hole-predominant catheters are preferred for high-flow pump injection in tiny branches
End-hole-only selective catheters are useful for diagnostic angiography and embolisation procedures
Side-plus-end-hole selective catheters can tolerate pump-injected runs better
Side-plus-end-hole selective catheters should not be used for embolotherapy because material can exit side holes or become trapped
updates.explanation: The source distinguishes end-hole-only catheters, which are hand-injection tools useful for angiography and embolisation, from side-plus-end-hole catheters, which can handle pump runs. Embolotherapy through side-hole catheters is unsafe because embolic material may lodge in side holes or leave through the wrong hole, causing non-target embolisation.

updates.question_text: Regarding catheter selection by vessel take-off angle, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Recurved catheters are mainly for straight vessels with no branch angle
Acute-angle vessels such as aortic arch branches favour angled-tip catheters
All renal and mesenteric selections require a pigtail catheter only
Catheter shape is unrelated to vessel take-off angle
Obtuse-angle vessels may favour recurved catheters such as Sidewinder/Simmons or Sos Omni
options_after: Recurved catheters are mainly for straight vessels without branch angle
Acute-angle vessels such as aortic arch branches favour angled-tip catheters
Most renal and mesenteric selections require a pigtail catheter
Catheter shape is unrelated to vessel take-off angle
Obtuse-angle vessels may favour recurved catheters such as Sidewinder/Simmons or Sos Omni
updates.explanation: The source uses take-off angle as the practical selection framework. Acute-angle branch vessels may favour angled-tip catheters, while obtuse-angle vessels may favour recurved catheters such as Sidewinder/Simmons or Sos Omni. Pigtails are flush catheters and catheter shape is highly related to vessel geometry.

updates.question_text: Regarding curved and recurved catheter concepts, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: A regular curved catheter has primary and secondary curves in the same direction in the source explanation
Recurved catheters are deployed by pushing them directly forward into every acute branch
A recurved catheter has primary and secondary curves in opposite directions
Recurved catheters are useful for vessels with obtuse take-off angles
Recurve terminology refers to guidewire J-tip radius
options_after: A regular curved catheter has primary and secondary curves in the same direction in the source explanation
Recurved catheters are deployed by pushing them directly forward into most acute branches
A recurved catheter has primary and secondary curves in opposite directions
Recurved catheters are useful for vessels with obtuse take-off angles
Recurve terminology refers to guidewire J-tip radius
updates.explanation: The source explains recurved catheters by comparing the direction of primary and secondary curves. Recurved catheters have opposing curves and are useful for obtuse vessel take-off, often by pulling back to drop into the branch. J-tip radius is guidewire terminology, not the definition of a recurved catheter.

updates.question_text: Regarding catheter-system terminology, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: A coaxial system means one catheter inside another catheter or sheath
A guide catheter is a larger catheter used to guide access toward the desired vessel
A vascular sheath is only a guidewire without a hemostatic valve
An introducer guide is another name for a long sheath in the source
Microcatheters are small catheters useful for tiny vessel superselection
options_after: A coaxial system means one catheter inside another catheter or sheath
A guide catheter is a larger catheter used to guide access toward the desired vessel
A vascular sheath is primarily a guidewire without a hemostatic valve
An introducer guide is another name for a long sheath in the source
Microcatheters are small catheters useful for tiny vessel superselection
updates.explanation: The source defines coaxial systems as one catheter within another catheter or sheath. Guide catheters and introducer guides/long sheaths help position and support more distal work. Microcatheters are small catheters used for tiny vessel superselection. A vascular sheath includes the tube, hemostatic valve and side-arm flushing access.

updates.question_text: Regarding angiographic flow-rate planning, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Hand arteries tolerate the same blood displacement as the spleen
Bigger arteries generally require higher injection rates
Flow rate is independent of catheter size and pressure tolerance
Venous phase interest never affects contrast volume planning
The goal is to displace enough blood to obtain an adequate image
options_after: Hand arteries tolerate the same blood displacement as the spleen
Bigger arteries generally require higher injection rates
Flow rate is independent of catheter size and pressure tolerance
Venous phase interest will not affect contrast volume planning
The goal is to displace enough blood to obtain an adequate image
updates.explanation: The source gives the practical rule that larger arteries require higher injection rates and that adequate imaging requires displacing a meaningful fraction of blood flow. Real-world planning also depends on catheter size, pressure tolerance, vessel size, distal bed volume and whether venous phase information is needed. Small distal beds tolerate less displacement than large vascular beds.

updates.question_text: Regarding typical angiographic injection-rate hierarchy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Bronchial and intercostal arteries are the highest-rate injections in the source table
The IMA always uses the same volume as a bronchial artery run
Aortic and pulmonary artery injections are high-rate injections compared with bronchial or intercostal artery injections
Aorta and carotid injections are assigned identical flow rates in the source table
Injection planning ignores distal vascular bed size
options_after: Bronchial and intercostal arteries are the highest-rate injections in the source table
The IMA characteristically uses the same volume as a bronchial artery run
Aortic and pulmonary artery injections are high-rate injections compared with bronchial or intercostal artery injections
Aorta and carotid injections are assigned closely comparable flow rates in the source table
Injection planning ignores distal vascular bed size
updates.explanation: The source table places aorta, aortic arch, IVC and pulmonary artery injections in the highest-rate group, while bronchial and intercostal arteries are low-rate small-vessel injections. Mesenteric vessels may use higher volumes when venous phase information is important. Distal bed size remains part of the planning logic.

updates.question_text: Regarding flow-rate determinants and catheter French size, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Maximum flow depends on internal diameter
Larger French size always lowers the maximum flow rate in the source practical rule
Maximum flow depends on catheter length
Maximum flow depends on the number of side holes
Maximum flow depends only on the labelled catheter length
options_after: Maximum flow depends on internal diameter
Larger French size characteristically lowers the maximum flow rate in the source practical rule
Maximum flow depends on catheter length
Maximum flow depends on the number of side holes
Maximum flow depends primarily on the labelled catheter length
updates.explanation: The source says maximum flow rates are determined by internal diameter, catheter length and side-hole design. Larger French size generally permits higher, not lower, flow in the source practical rule. Labelled length alone is not sufficient to determine maximum flow.

updates.question_text: Regarding practical catheter and wire safety rules, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Keep hydrophilic wires wet during manipulation
Avoid steering stiff wires around curves without catheter support
Use the stiffest wire first to cross every tight vessel
Use a test injection before full injection through a pigtail catheter
Avoid embolotherapy through side-hole catheters
options_after: Keep hydrophilic wires wet during manipulation
Avoid steering stiff wires around curves without catheter support
Use the stiffest wire first to cross a tight vessel
Use a test injection before full injection through a pigtail catheter
Avoid embolotherapy through side-hole catheters
updates.explanation: These are the source's practical safety themes: hydrophilic wires work wet, stiff wires need catheter support, pigtail position should be checked before full injection, and side-hole catheters are unsafe for embolotherapy. Tight vessel crossing usually favours hydrophilic/steerable access rather than starting with the stiffest rail.

updates.question_text: Regarding the most practical takeaways from this instrument section, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Know whether the size number refers to inner or outer diameter
All labelled size systems in IR use the same physical convention
Catheter hole configuration is irrelevant to embolotherapy safety
Choose wire stiffness and catheter shape according to the access problem
Flow-rate planning ignores vessel size
options_after: Know whether the size number refers to inner or outer diameter
Most labelled size systems in IR use the same physical convention
Catheter hole configuration is irrelevant to embolotherapy safety
Choose wire stiffness and catheter shape according to the access problem
Flow-rate planning ignores vessel size
updates.explanation: The central practical points are size-system literacy and tool selection. Needles, catheters and sheaths use different conventions, so inner versus outer diameter matters. Wire stiffness, catheter shape and catheter hole configuration all affect procedural safety and task selection. Flow planning also depends on vessel and catheter characteristics.

updates.question_text: Regarding flushing troubleshooting, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: If aspiration fails, forcefully flush clot into any cerebral catheter as the default next step
If blood is accidentally mixed into the saline syringe, discard it and double flush
Failure to aspirate proves the catheter is safely positioned for high-flow injection
Blood-saline mixing is required before every catheter injection
If no blood can be aspirated, first manipulate or pull back because the catheter may be against a wall
options_after: If aspiration fails, forcefully flush clot into any cerebral catheter as the default next step
If blood is accidentally mixed into the saline syringe, discard it and double flush
Failure to aspirate proves the catheter is safely positioned for high-flow injection
Blood-saline mixing is required before catheter injection
If no blood can be aspirated, first manipulate or pull back because the catheter may be against a wall
updates.explanation: The source says that if blood and saline are accidentally mixed, the syringe should be discarded and a double flush performed. If blood cannot be aspirated, the first assumption is catheter-wall apposition, so repositioning or pulling back is tried. Persistent failure raises concern for clot; forcefully flushing it is not the default safe action except in limited situations such as embolising that location.

updates.question_text: Regarding high femoral arterial puncture, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: High puncture primarily causes distal embolisation from plaque
High puncture is preferred because it compresses better against the femoral head
A puncture above the inguinal ligament increases the risk of retroperitoneal bleeding
High puncture protects against all access-site bleeding
High puncture is the standard goal for routine femoral arterial access
options_after: High puncture primarily causes distal embolisation from plaque
High puncture is preferred because it compresses better against the femoral head
A puncture above the inguinal ligament increases the risk of retroperitoneal bleeding
High puncture protects against most access-site bleeding
High puncture is the standard goal for routine femoral arterial access
updates.explanation: The source highlights high puncture above the inguinal ligament as the access mistake that risks retroperitoneal bleeding. The preferred target is over the femoral head, below the inguinal ligament/inferior epigastric artery and above the common femoral bifurcation, where compression is possible.

updates.question_text: Regarding brachial arterial access, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It can be useful when femoral access is unavailable
It carries higher stroke risk than femoral access when catheters cross the arch/great vessels
Holding pressure is always easier than at the femoral artery
It can be useful for upper limb angioplasty
A small haematoma in this location cannot threaten the hand
options_after: It can be useful when femoral access is unavailable
It carries higher stroke risk than femoral access when catheters cross the arch/great vessels
Holding pressure is characteristically easier than at the femoral artery
It can be useful for upper limb angioplasty
A small haematoma in this location will not threaten the hand
updates.explanation: The source lists inaccessible femoral access and upper limb angioplasty as reasons to use brachial access. It also warns that pressure can be difficult, even small haematomas can cause medial brachial fascial compartment syndrome, and stroke risk is higher when the catheter must traverse the great vessels/arch.

updates.question_text: Regarding arm choice for brachial access, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The left arm is favoured when heading toward the abdominal aorta or lower extremity
If all else is equal, the right arm is favoured in the source
A systolic blood pressure difference greater than 20 should be ignored when choosing the arm
The right arm is favoured when heading toward the thoracic aorta or cerebral vessels
The source recommends always choosing the right arm regardless of target
options_after: The left arm is favoured when heading toward the abdominal aorta or lower extremity
If most else is equal, the right arm is favoured in the source
A systolic blood pressure difference greater than 20 should be ignored when choosing the arm
The right arm is favoured when heading toward the thoracic aorta or cerebral vessels
The source recommends characteristically choosing the right arm despite variation in target
updates.explanation: The source's practical rule is left arm for heading south and right arm for heading north. If all else is equal, left is favoured because it is often non-dominant and avoids more cerebral vessels. A significant systolic pressure difference suggests stenosis and should change the access plan rather than being ignored.

updates.question_text: Regarding translumbar aortic puncture, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Psoas haematoma is impossible because the needle avoids the psoas
It is performed prone in the source description
A left-sided approach helps avoid the IVC
Known supraceliac aortic aneurysm is an indication rather than a contraindication
The patient self-compresses after the procedure by rolling supine
options_after: The psoas is excluded from needle-related haematoma risk
It is performed prone in the source description
A left-sided approach helps avoid the IVC
Known supraceliac aortic aneurysm is an indication rather than a contraindication
The patient self-compresses after the procedure by rolling supine
updates.explanation: Translumbar aortic puncture is described as prone and often left-sided to avoid the IVC. Afterward, the patient rolls supine to self-compress. The needle path crosses the psoas and haematoma is common. Known supraceliac aortic aneurysm is listed as a contraindication.

updates.question_text: Regarding translumbar aortic puncture contraindications, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Mild backache after the procedure proves cord infarction
The approach is usually performed supine through the anterior abdomen
Known supraceliac aortic aneurysm is a contraindication in the source
The needle path never crosses muscle
The source states that it is the routine first-line access for all angiography
options_after: Mild backache after the procedure proves cord infarction
The approach is usually performed supine through the anterior abdomen
Known supraceliac aortic aneurysm is a contraindication in the source
The needle path will not cross muscle
The source states that it is the routine first-line access for most angiography
updates.explanation: The useful contraindication from the source is known supraceliac aortic aneurysm. The procedure is prone and posterior, with a needle path crossing the psoas. A mild backache is expected from psoas haematoma in the source framing and does not by itself prove cord infarction.

updates.question_text: Regarding pre-procedure arterial access preparation in the source, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Heparin is stopped before the procedure in the source protocol
An INR around 1.5 is the value the source would choose if asked
Diagnostic angiography, routine angioplasty and thrombolysis are considered contaminated procedures requiring prophylactic antibiotics in the cited ACR framing
Platelet count should be above at least 50,000 in the source
Antibiotic prophylaxis is mandatory for all diagnostic angiography
options_after: Heparin is stopped before the procedure in the source protocol
An INR around 1.5 is the value the source would choose if asked
Diagnostic angiography, routine angioplasty and thrombolysis are considered contaminated procedures requiring prophylactic antibiotics in the cited ACR framing
Platelet count should be above at least 50,000 in the source
Antibiotic prophylaxis is mandatory for most diagnostic angiography
updates.explanation: The source includes stopping heparin pre-procedure, using about INR 1.5 as a practical threshold, and having platelets above at least 50,000. It also states that diagnostic angiography, routine angioplasty and thrombolysis are considered clean procedures, so antibiotic prophylaxis is unnecessary. That makes mandatory antibiotics incorrect.

updates.question_text: Regarding post-procedure arterial access care, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Heparin can be restarted immediately without regard to access-site complications
Closure devices are used when infection at the access site is suspected
Manual compression is described as about 15 minutes by the book
A sheath should never be pulled at any ACT below 300
Groin check and pulse palpation should be included in post-procedure orders
options_after: Heparin can be restarted immediately without regard to access-site complications
Closure devices are used when infection at the access site is suspected
Manual compression is described as about 15 minutes by the book
A sheath should not be pulled at any ACT below 300
Groin check and pulse palpation should be included in post-procedure orders
updates.explanation: The source lists about 15 minutes of compression, groin check and pulse palpation as post-procedure care points. Heparin restart is delayed and assumes no complications. Closure devices should not be used when access-site infection is suspected. Sheath removal is discussed at lower ACT thresholds than 300.

updates.question_text: Regarding dialysis catheter access, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Right internal jugular vein is preferred
Subclavian thrombosis has no consequence for arm drainage in the source
The cavoatrial junction is the preferred catheter tip location in the source
Right IJ offers a short route to the cavoatrial junction
Femoral access is preferred over right IJ for long-term dialysis access
options_after: Right internal jugular vein is preferred
Subclavian thrombosis lacks consequence for arm drainage in the source
The cavoatrial junction is the preferred catheter tip location in the source
Right IJ offers a short route to the cavoatrial junction
Femoral access is preferred over right IJ for long-term dialysis access
updates.explanation: Right IJ is preferred because it provides a short route to the cavoatrial junction and has a lower thrombosis penalty than subclavian access. If subclavian thromboses, arm drainage can be compromised. Femoral access is less desirable, especially because of groin contamination risk.

updates.question_text: Regarding post-access hypotension and bleeding, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Hypotension after femoral access proves a small superficial haematoma only
Hypotension after arterial access should raise concern for high stick and retroperitoneal bleeding
The skin puncture and arterial puncture are always directly aligned
Antegrade and retrograde punctures require identical compression location
An angioplasty balloon across the bleeding or inflow vessel may help control bleeding
options_after: Hypotension after femoral access proves a small superficial haematoma
Hypotension after arterial access should raise concern for high stick and retroperitoneal bleeding
The skin puncture and arterial puncture are characteristically directly aligned
Antegrade and retrograde punctures require closely comparable compression location
An angioplasty balloon across the bleeding or inflow vessel may help control bleeding
updates.explanation: The source links hypotension after arterial access to high puncture and possible retroperitoneal bleeding. Temporising control can include balloon occlusion across the bleeding or inflow vessel. Skin and arterial holes do not necessarily align, so compression location depends on antegrade versus retrograde puncture geometry.

updates.question_text: Regarding access-site pseudoaneurysm recognition and treatment, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Pain out of proportion after a percutaneous stick should prompt ultrasound evaluation for pseudoaneurysm
Open surgery is the only repair option discussed for access-site pseudoaneurysm
Small pseudoaneurysms can undergo spontaneous thrombosis
Long narrow neck and small defect favour interventional therapy success
Pseudoaneurysm is excluded if the patient had a cardiac catheterisation
options_after: Pain out of proportion after a percutaneous stick should prompt ultrasound evaluation for pseudoaneurysm
Open surgery is the principal repair option discussed for access-site pseudoaneurysm
Small pseudoaneurysms can undergo spontaneous thrombosis
Long narrow neck and small defect favour interventional therapy success
Pseudoaneurysm is excluded if the patient had a cardiac catheterisation
updates.explanation: The source says disproportionate pain after a percutaneous stick should trigger ultrasound for pseudoaneurysm. Small lesions can thrombose spontaneously, and long narrow necks/small defects respond better to intervention. Repair options include surgery, direct ultrasound compression and thrombin injection rather than surgery alone. Cardiac catheterisation is a classic setting for pseudoaneurysm.

updates.question_text: Regarding pseudoaneurysm management choices, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: A wide neck favours thrombin injection safety and success
Infection pushes management toward surgery rather than thrombin/compression
Active bleeding or skin necrosis are concerning features favouring surgical management
Large neck size always improves thrombin safety
A small cavity can be followed with repeat ultrasound in selected cases
options_after: A wide neck favours thrombin injection safety and success
Infection pushes management toward surgery rather than thrombin/compression
Active bleeding or skin necrosis are concerning features favouring surgical management
Large neck size characteristically improves thrombin safety
A small cavity can be followed with repeat ultrasound in selected cases
updates.explanation: The source algorithm escalates infected, actively bleeding or skin-necrotic cases toward surgery. Small lesions can be followed, and narrow-neck morphology favours thrombin injection. A wide neck increases risk of thrombin propagation and lowers success of compression/injection strategies.

updates.question_text: Regarding angioplasty indications and endpoints, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: A general indication is more than 50% stenosis with symptoms
Symptoms are irrelevant to the source's general angioplasty indication
A balloon should intentionally be much smaller than the normal vessel
Residual stenosis less than 30% is often considered procedural success
All residual narrowing mandates stenting even without a pressure gradient
options_after: A general indication is more than 50% stenosis with symptoms
Symptoms are irrelevant to the source's general angioplasty indication
A balloon should intentionally be much smaller than the normal vessel
Residual stenosis less than 30% is often considered procedural success
Most residual narrowing mandates stenting even without a pressure gradient
updates.explanation: The source gives symptomatic greater-than-50% stenosis as the general angioplasty indication and less-than-30% residual stenosis as a common success threshold. Symptoms matter. Balloon sizing should approximate the adjacent normal vessel with modest oversizing, and residual stenosis without a pressure gradient may still be acceptable.

updates.question_text: Regarding stent selection, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Balloon-expandable stents are poor for precise deployment in the source
Self-expanding stents are useful in superficial areas that may be compressed
Renal ostium is the source's classic self-expanding stent example
Self-expanding stents are the precise-deployment choice for every renal ostial lesion
Cervical carotid and SFA are classic self-expanding stent examples in the source
options_after: Balloon-expandable stents are poor for precise deployment in the source
Self-expanding stents are useful in superficial areas that may be compressed
Renal ostium is the source's classic self-expanding stent example
Self-expanding stents are the precise-deployment choice for most renal ostial lesions
Cervical carotid and SFA are classic self-expanding stent examples in the source
updates.explanation: The source chooses self-expanding stents for superficial or compressible regions such as cervical carotid and SFA. Balloon-expandable stents provide more precise deployment, with renal ostium as the classic balloon-expandable example. Therefore renal ostial precision is not the self-expanding example.

updates.question_text: Regarding balloon and stent sizing, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Balloons should be about 10-20% larger than adjacent normal vessel diameter
Post-stenotic dilatation should not be used as the sizing reference
Larger balloons increase dilating force but also increase risk of rupture or dissection
Balloons should be selected from the narrowest part of the stenosis only
Stents are generally selected slightly longer and wider than the lesion/vessel target
options_after: Balloons should be about 10-20% larger than adjacent normal vessel diameter
Post-stenotic dilatation should not be used as the sizing reference
Larger balloons increase dilating force but also increase risk of rupture or dissection
Balloons should be selected from the narrowest part of the stenosis
Stents are generally selected slightly longer and wider than the lesion/vessel target
updates.explanation: The source recommends balloon sizing from adjacent normal non-stenotic vessel, usually 10-20% oversized. Post-stenotic dilatation is a trap for oversizing. Larger balloons provide more force but increase rupture/dissection risk. Stents are sized slightly longer than the stenosis and slightly wider than the normal lumen.

updates.question_text: Regarding persistent residual stenosis after angioplasty, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Residual stenosis without gradient always mandates immediate covered stent placement
If residual stenosis is more than 30%, first measure a pressure gradient if possible
The next step is never to measure a gradient
If there is no pressure gradient, the operator may still stop and accept the result in the source
If there is a gradient from elastic recoil, stenting is the next step
options_after: Residual stenosis without gradient characteristically mandates immediate covered stent placement
If residual stenosis is more than 30%, first measure a pressure gradient if possible
The next step is not to measure a gradient
If there is no pressure gradient, the operator may still stop and accept the result in the source
If there is a gradient from elastic recoil, stenting is the next step
updates.explanation: The source's approach is to measure a gradient when residual stenosis remains. Without a gradient, stopping may be acceptable. If the lesion disappears with balloon inflation but recoils with a gradient after deflation, stenting is the next step. Immediate stenting without physiologic assessment is not the default when a gradient can be measured.

updates.question_text: Regarding angioplasty complications and immediate management, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: If a balloon waist will not efface, a higher-pressure or cutting balloon can be considered
Extravasation after angioplasty is managed by removing all balloons and waiting without tamponade
If distal embolisation occurs, first perform an angiographic run to assess distal vessels
Leaving the balloon on the wire after angioplasty has no value if rupture occurs
Distal embolisation always requires treatment even if the distal limb vessels look normal
options_after: If a balloon waist will not efface, a higher-pressure or cutting balloon can be considered
Extravasation after angioplasty is managed by removing most balloons and waiting without tamponade
If distal embolisation occurs, first perform an angiographic run to assess distal vessels
Leaving the balloon on the wire after angioplasty lacks value if rupture occurs
Distal embolisation characteristically requires treatment even if the distal limb vessels look normal
updates.explanation: The source recommends higher-pressure or cutting balloon when the waist will not efface, and angiographic assessment after distal embolisation. If distal vessels look fine, no intervention may be needed; threatened limb prompts clot aspiration. Extravasation is managed by getting the balloon back in place for low-pressure tamponade, which is why the balloon is left on the wire after angioplasty.

updates.question_text: Regarding EVAR indications, anatomy and complications, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: AAA larger than 5 cm or rapidly enlarging AAA is an EVAR indication in the source
Covering a critical artery needed for perfusion is acceptable during infrarenal EVAR in the source
The proximal landing zone should be long enough, non-aneurysmal and not excessively angulated
Extensive aortic coverage protects against spinal cord ischaemia, so new paraplegia symptoms require no urgent action
Juxtarenal aneurysm means a long healthy neck far from the renal arteries
options_after: AAA larger than 5 cm or rapidly enlarging AAA is an EVAR indication in the source
Covering a critical artery needed for perfusion is acceptable during infrarenal EVAR in the source
The proximal landing zone should be long enough, non-aneurysmal and not excessively angulated
New paraplegia after extensive aortic coverage can be observed without urgent intervention
Juxtarenal aneurysm means a long healthy neck far from the renal arteries
updates.explanation: The source gives EVAR indications including AAA larger than 5 cm or rapid growth, and requires a suitable proximal landing zone. Covering a critical artery can be an absolute contraindication, and extensive aortic coverage can cause spinal cord ischaemia with CSF drainage as an urgent response to developing paraplegia symptoms. Juxtarenal aneurysm implies a short neck or encroachment on the renal arteries, not a long healthy neck.

updates.question_text: Regarding type 2 endoleak, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: It is always treated emergently even if the sac is stable
It is the most common endoleak type in the source
It is high-pressure inflow from an inadequate proximal seal
It is caused by fabric porosity in modern grafts
IMA and lumbar arteries are typical culprit feeders
options_after: It is characteristically treated emergently even if the sac is stable
It is the most common endoleak type in the source
It is high-pressure inflow from an inadequate proximal seal
It is caused by fabric porosity in modern grafts
IMA and lumbar arteries are typical culprit feeders
updates.explanation: Type 2 endoleak is the commonest type and is usually due to collateral sac filling from vessels such as the IMA or lumbar arteries. The source states that most are observed initially, following sac size, and treated if the sac grows. High-pressure seal-zone leak is type 1; porosity is type 4.

updates.question_text: Regarding endoleak treatment urgency, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Type 1 endoleak is high pressure and requires intervention
Most type 4 endoleaks persist indefinitely and require emergent treatment in the source
Type 3 endoleak is high flow and requires intervention
Stable type 2 endoleak is commonly observed initially
Type 2 endoleak must always be treated before type 1 endoleak
options_after: Type 1 endoleak is high pressure and requires intervention
Most type 4 endoleaks persist indefinitely and require emergent treatment in the source
Type 3 endoleak is high flow and requires intervention
Stable type 2 endoleak is commonly observed initially
Type 2 endoleak must characteristically be treated before type 1 endoleak
updates.explanation: The source identifies type 1 and type 3 as high-flow/high-pressure endoleaks needing urgent treatment. Type 2 is often watched if the sac is not enlarging. Type 4 is usually early porosity and often resolves within 48 hours rather than persisting indefinitely. Type 2 is not prioritised above type 1.

updates.question_text: Regarding broad embolisation strategy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Embolisation can be used to stop bleeding
Embolisation can be used to devascularise tumours
The source states that all embolic agents are interchangeable
Agent choice depends on desired outcome and risk minimisation
The choice differs when temporary versus permanent occlusion is desired
options_after: Embolisation can be used to stop bleeding
Embolisation can be used to devascularise tumours
The source states that most embolic agents are interchangeable
Agent choice depends on desired outcome and risk minimisation
The choice differs when temporary versus permanent occlusion is desired
updates.explanation: The source frames embolisation around goals such as stopping bleeding and killing or devascularising tumour. Agent choice depends on target vessel size, desired temporary/permanent effect, and non-target risk. Embolic agents are not interchangeable because proximal, distal, temporary and permanent effects differ.

updates.question_text: Regarding proximal versus distal embolic strategy, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Large proximal embolics are preferred when the goal is complete tissue infarction at the arteriole level
Distal embolics are used only for temporary occlusion of large arteries
Distal small-particle embolisation is used when the goal is to infarct tissue
Proximal embolics always preserve future reaccess
Particle size has no relationship to tissue necrosis risk
options_after: Large proximal embolics are preferred when the goal is complete tissue infarction at the arteriole level
Distal embolics are used primarily for temporary occlusion of large arteries
Distal small-particle embolisation is used when the goal is to infarct tissue
Proximal embolics characteristically preserve future reaccess
Particle size lacks relationship to tissue necrosis risk
updates.explanation: The source distinguishes proximal flow reduction from distal tissue infarction. Distal embolics such as small particles can occlude arterioles and infarct tissue, which is useful for tumour ablation but increases non-target injury risk. Large proximal embolics are used to slow or block flow in larger vessels rather than to reach capillary beds.

updates.question_text: Regarding mechanical embolic agents, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: An Amplatzer vascular plug is a temporary gelfoam slurry rather than a nitinol mesh
Coils are typically used for permanent occlusion of a large vessel
Coils are the preferred agent for all future-reaccess bronchial artery embolisations
Mechanical agents are designed for capillary-level temporary occlusion
Vascular plugs can be useful for high-flow single large-vessel occlusion
options_after: An Amplatzer vascular plug is a temporary gelfoam slurry rather than a nitinol mesh
Coils are typically used for permanent occlusion of a large vessel
Coils are the preferred agent for most future-reaccess bronchial artery embolisations
Mechanical agents are designed for capillary-level temporary occlusion
Vascular plugs can be useful for high-flow single large-vessel occlusion
updates.explanation: The source describes coils as permanent large-vessel occlusion tools and Amplatzer vascular plugs as self-expanding nitinol devices useful in high-flow single-vessel settings. Bronchial arteries may rebleed and need future access, so coils are avoided there. Mechanical agents are not capillary-level temporary embolics.

updates.question_text: Regarding coil deployment, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Accurate deployment is associated with detachable coils in the source
Microcoils are deployed through standard catheters rather than microcatheters
Coils should be delivered through an end-hole catheter for accurate deployment
Coils should not be deployed through a side-hole plus end-hole catheter
Microcoils should be deployed through a standard catheter because they cannot clog it
options_after: Accurate deployment is associated with detachable coils in the source
Microcoils are deployed through standard catheters rather than microcatheters
Coils should be delivered through an end-hole catheter for accurate deployment
Coils should not be deployed through a side-hole plus end-hole catheter
Microcoils should be deployed through a standard catheter because they will not clog it
updates.explanation: The source links accurate deployment with detachable coils and warns against deploying coils through side-hole catheters. Coils require end-hole-only delivery when precision matters. Microcoils belong through microcatheters; through a standard catheter they can ball up and clog the catheter.

updates.question_text: Regarding stopping particle embolisation, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The operator should keep injecting particles until reflux is seen
The classic endpoint is when flow becomes to-and-fro
To-and-fro flow proves the particles are in the venous system
Particle embolisation has no endpoint
Continuing until complete occlusion may risk reflux into non-target vessels
options_after: The operator should keep injecting particles until reflux is seen
The classic endpoint is when flow becomes to-and-fro
To-and-fro flow proves the particles are in the venous system
Particle embolisation lacks endpoint
Continuing until complete occlusion may risk reflux into non-target vessels
updates.explanation: The source teaches stopping particle embolisation when flow becomes to-and-fro. Continuing until complete occlusion increases reflux risk and potential non-target embolisation. To-and-fro flow is an arterial embolisation endpoint, not proof of venous particle passage.

updates.question_text: Regarding balloon occlusion during sclerosant embolisation, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: The balloon should be deflated immediately without aspiration after alcohol injection
Balloon occlusion is used only to diagnose carotid stenosis
Balloon occlusion can protect non-target sites
Aspiration after balloon occlusion increases non-target embolisation risk in the source
Before deflating the balloon, aggressive aspiration is performed to clear residual sclerosant
options_after: The balloon should be deflated immediately without aspiration after alcohol injection
Balloon occlusion is used primarily to diagnose carotid stenosis
Balloon occlusion can protect non-target sites
Aspiration after balloon occlusion increases non-target embolisation risk in the source
Before deflating the balloon, aggressive aspiration is performed to clear residual sclerosant
updates.explanation: The source presents balloon occlusion as one way to protect non-target sites during sclerosant use. Before deflation, aggressive aspiration is performed to remove residual agent. Immediate deflation without aspiration is unsafe.

updates.question_text: Regarding non-sclerosant liquid embolic agents, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Onyx dries slowly from outside inward and allows slower, controlled delivery
Onyx is used in neuro procedures and hypervascular spine tumours in the source
Ethiodol is invisible on imaging and cannot be used for follow-up assessment
Ethiodol is radiopaque
Ethiodol preferentially flows to hepatoma in the source
options_after: Onyx dries slowly from outside inward and allows slower, controlled delivery
Onyx is used in neuro procedures and hypervascular spine tumours in the source
Ethiodol is invisible on imaging and will not be used for follow-up assessment
Ethiodol is radiopaque
Ethiodol preferentially flows to hepatoma in the source
updates.explanation: Onyx is described as a slow-drying non-sclerosant useful for controlled delivery, especially in neuro and hypervascular spine tumour settings. Ethiodol is radiopaque and preferentially flows to hepatomas, helping reduce non-target embolisation and track tumour size on follow-up. It is not invisible.

updates.question_text: Regarding post-embolisation syndrome, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Pain, nausea, vomiting and low-grade fever are expected findings
Post-embolisation syndrome is limited to fibroid embolisation and does not occur after solid organ tumour embolisation
The syndrome commonly starts within the first few days and resolves within a few days
Large fibroid embolisation is a classic vignette setting
Blood cultures are mandatory in every case without other infection signs
options_after: Pain, nausea, vomiting and low-grade fever are expected findings
Post-embolisation syndrome is limited to fibroid embolisation and does not occur after solid organ tumour embolisation
The syndrome commonly starts within the first few days and resolves within a few days
Large fibroid embolisation is a classic vignette setting
Blood cultures are mandatory in most cases without other infection signs
updates.explanation: The source describes post-embolisation syndrome as expected pain, nausea, vomiting and low-grade fever, often beginning within three days and resolving within three days after starting. It is classically seen after large fibroid embolisation and can occur after large solid-organ tumour embolisation. Blood cultures are not needed without other factors suggesting infection.

updates.question_text: Regarding acute limb ischaemia embolus locations, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: More distal emboli cannot produce blue toe syndrome in the source
Emboli commonly lodge at the common femoral bifurcation or popliteal trifurcation
The source states that acute limb ischaemia is never embolic
Blue toe syndrome requires aortic root aneurysm
Popliteal trifurcation emboli are unrelated to acute limb ischaemia
options_after: More distal emboli will not produce blue toe syndrome in the source
Emboli commonly lodge at the common femoral bifurcation or popliteal trifurcation
The source states that acute limb ischaemia is not embolic
Blue toe syndrome requires aortic root aneurysm
Popliteal trifurcation emboli are unrelated to acute limb ischaemia
updates.explanation: The source states that emboli often lodge at bifurcations such as the common femoral bifurcation and popliteal trifurcation, and more distal emboli can cause blue toe syndrome. Acute limb ischaemia can be thrombotic or embolic. Aortic root aneurysm is not required for blue toe syndrome.

updates.question_text: Regarding critical limb ischaemia and acute limb treatment logic, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Lysis cures all underlying arterial disease permanently
Critical limb ischaemia includes rest pain for two weeks, ulceration or gangrene in the source
Thrombolysis re-establishes baseline flow, so additional angioplasty/stent/surgery may still be needed
Outflow disease must always be treated before inflow disease
If inflow and outflow disease coexist, treating inflow first is favoured
options_after: Lysis cures most underlying arterial disease permanently
Critical limb ischaemia includes rest pain for two weeks, ulceration or gangrene in the source
Thrombolysis re-establishes baseline flow, so additional angioplasty/stent/surgery may still be needed
Outflow disease must characteristically be treated before inflow disease
If inflow and outflow disease coexist, treating inflow first is favoured
updates.explanation: The source defines critical limb ischaemia using rest pain for two weeks, ulceration or gangrene. Lysis clears clot only to baseline, which may still be poor, so angioplasty, surgery or stenting may be needed. When both inflow and outflow disease are present, inflow is treated first.

updates.question_text: Regarding surgery versus thrombolysis for acute limb ischaemia in the source, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Occlusion for less than 14 days favours thrombolysis
Fragmented distal emboli should never receive endovascular thrombolytic therapy in the ACR framing
Isolated suprainguinal embolism is usually thrombolysed rather than surgically removed in the source summary
Occlusion for more than 14 days favours surgery
Duration of occlusion is irrelevant to treatment choice
options_after: Occlusion for less than 14 days favours thrombolysis
Fragmented distal emboli should not receive endovascular thrombolytic therapy in the ACR framing
Isolated suprainguinal embolism is usually thrombolysed rather than surgically removed in the source summary
Occlusion for more than 14 days favours surgery
Duration of occlusion is irrelevant to treatment choice
updates.explanation: The source gives the broad rule that thrombolysis is superior when occlusion duration is under 14 days, while surgery is superior beyond 14 days. It also notes ACR-style distinctions such as distal fragmented emboli favouring thrombolysis and isolated suprainguinal embolism favouring surgery. Duration is therefore relevant.

updates.question_text: Regarding segmental pressures and arterial waveforms, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: A pressure drop across thigh, calf or ankle segments can help localise disease level
Segmental pressures cannot provide any localisation information
Normal peripheral arterial waveform is triphasic because of systolic forward flow and diastolic rebound
Loss of vessel compliance contributes to progressive waveform degradation
Triphasic waveform requires venous reflux
options_after: A pressure drop across thigh, calf or ankle segments can help localise disease level
Segmental pressures will not provide any localisation information
Normal peripheral arterial waveform is triphasic because of systolic forward flow and diastolic rebound
Loss of vessel compliance contributes to progressive waveform degradation
Triphasic waveform requires venous reflux
updates.explanation: Segmental pressures can suggest disease level when a significant pressure drop is found. Normal peripheral arterial waveform is triphasic, reflecting systolic forward flow and rebound from the high-resistance distal vascular bed. As vessels become less compliant, the waveform becomes more abnormal. Venous reflux is unrelated.

updates.question_text: Regarding ulcer location trivia in the source, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Dorsum of foot ulcer suggests ischaemic or infected ulcer
Medial ankle ulcer suggests venous stasis
Plantar surface ulcer suggests neurotrophic ulcer
Plantar ulcers are the classic site for venous stasis
Medial ankle ulcers are always neurotrophic
options_after: Dorsum of foot ulcer suggests ischaemic or infected ulcer
Medial ankle ulcer suggests venous stasis
Plantar surface ulcer suggests neurotrophic ulcer
Plantar ulcers are the classic site for venous stasis
Medial ankle ulcers are characteristically neurotrophic
updates.explanation: The source lists medial ankle as the classic venous stasis ulcer location. Dorsum of foot is associated with ischaemic or infected ulcers, and plantar surface with neurotrophic ulcers. The false alternatives reverse those associations.

updates.question_text: Regarding bypass graft patency terminology, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Secondary patency means patency was never lost
Repair of distal vessels or anastomotic vessels necessarily counts as loss of primary patency in the source
Primary patency means uninterrupted graft patency with no procedure on the graft itself
Secondary patency means the graft never occluded
Assisted primary patency means patency is maintained by prophylactic intervention before occlusion
options_after: Secondary patency means patency was not lost
Repair of distal vessels or anastomotic vessels necessarily counts as loss of primary patency in the source
Primary patency means uninterrupted graft patency with no procedure on the graft itself
Secondary patency means the graft has remained continuously patent
Assisted primary patency means patency is maintained by prophylactic intervention before occlusion
updates.explanation: Primary patency means the graft itself remains continuously patent without graft intervention. Assisted primary patency means patency is preserved by prophylactic treatment such as angioplasty before occlusion. Secondary patency means patency was lost and then restored. Distal or anastomotic vessel repair does not necessarily count as loss of primary graft patency in the source.

updates.question_text: Regarding catheter-directed thrombolysis troubleshooting, which of the following statements are correct?
options_before: Tachycardia and hypotension during TPA exclude bleeding and should not change management
If the clot cannot be crossed with a wire, organised clot is suggested and thrombolysis may not work
No clearing during check angiography suggests lytic stagnation and stopping is reasonable
Continuing thrombolysis beyond 48 hours is always preferred if any clot remains
New confusion during TPA infusion should raise concern for intracranial bleeding and prompt non-contrast CT head
options_after: Tachycardia and hypotension during TPA exclude bleeding and should not change management
If the clot cannot be crossed with a wire, organised clot is suggested and thrombolysis may not work
No clearing during check angiography suggests lytic stagnation and stopping is reasonable
